world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog lists only subclassification refs (Breen 2007, Bowern 2010); no published grammar/phonology of Ngamini located.

new_statements.quote: Bowern 2001:253: 'The stem of the second-person dual, PK *nhula, is probably related to PPN *NHuNpalV by syncope of the unstressed syllable (stress at all stages of Karnic is on the initial syllable of the word); clearly is it more likely that this change happened once, in a language which was ancestral to all Karnic languages, than individually, in each daughter language.' | Breen 2016:163: 'For example, thungka ‘rotten’ as [ˈt̪ʊŋgʷa], ngalkungka ‘1du.ex.DAT’ as [ˈŋalkʊŋgʷa] in Ngamini (in which this applies only to the velar stop)' ; 2016:165: 'Ngamini kurithidi ‘head’ pronounced [ˈgwijit̪iɾi].'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the first syllable, as in all Karnic languages (Bowern's family-wide statement); the principal Ngamini fieldworker's own IPA transcriptions of Ngamini words consistently mark primary stress on the initial syllable. No Ngamini-specific published rule statement exists; the full description (Breen's 2016 draft grammar) is unpublished.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated for Ngamini. (Closely related Diyari: secondary stress on the third vowel of a four-syllable root and on the first syllable of polysyllabic suffixes, Austin 2025 sec. 2.5; Yandruwandha similar, Breen 2004 sec. 3.6 -- not to be transferred without a source.)
new_statements.exceptions: None for Ngamini. Breen 2016:161-162 notes generally that Australian initial stress 'can move to a later syllable if that syllable has a long or a low vowel' as a diachronic tendency, not as a Ngamini rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Bowern's statement is about the (phonological) word, made in a comparative-reconstruction context for the whole Karnic subgroup, not from a description of Ngamini; Breen's evidence is citation-form phonetic transcriptions of three isolated words. Treat as family-level plus transcription evidence, low grade.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottocode ngam1265 bundles three varieties: Ngamini (ngam1284), Yarluyandi/Yaluyandi/Jeljendi (yarl1238, iso yry) and Karangura (kara1508). All modern data are Ngamini as spoken by Bob and Maudie Naylon (Birdsville; recorded by Breen 1967-76 and Austin 1975-76; Maudie Naylon's first language was Wangkangurru and she was also Hercus's main Yarluyandi consultant). Breen's 2016 transcriptions are Ngamini proper (ngam1284). Bowern's 2001 statement is for the Karnic subgroup as a whole. Karangura is attested only in 19th-century word lists (Austin 1991) and has no phonological description.

sources.note: p.253, parenthetical in the pronoun reconstruction: '(stress at all stages of Karnic is on the initial syllable of the word)'; p.256: nasal+stop clusters reduced to a nasal 'when preceded by an unstressed syllable'. Family-level (Karnic-wide) claim; Ngamini is classified as Central Karnic in the same paper. Not a Ngamini-specific description.

sources.citation: Austin, Peter K. 2025. A Grammar of Diyari, South Australia. 2nd edition, version 2.16 (MS, SOAS; PDF dated 2025-08-01). Also Austin 2021 v2.10 already on file at
sources.note: Sec. 2.5: Diyari primary stress on the first vowel of the root (initial), secondary stress by morpheme. Over 100 comparative notes on Ngamini and Yaluyandi drawn from Breen's recordings and Breen's 2016 draft grammar, but none concern Ngamini stress. Bibliography lists 'Breen, Gavan. 2016. The Ngamini language, as remembered by Bob and Maudie Naylon. Computer files.' and the preface thanks Breen for 'his unpublished draft grammar of Ngamini'.

sources.citation: Breen, Gavan. 2016. What's up with /u/. In P.K. Austin, H. Koch & J. Simpson (eds), Language, land & song: Studies in honour of Luise Hercus, 158-171. London: EL Publishing.
sources.note: pp.161-162: stress 'is typically on the first syllable of a word in Australia' (general). p.163 and p.165: Breen's own Ngamini phonetic transcriptions (from his unpublished field notes, fn.5) all carry primary stress on the first syllable: thungka 'rotten' [ˈt̪ʊŋgʷa], ngalkungka '1du.ex.DAT' [ˈŋalkʊŋgʷa], kurithidi 'head' [ˈgwijit̪iɾi]. No explicit Ngamini stress rule is stated.

sources.citation: Hercus, Luise A. 1994. A grammar of the Arabana-Wangkangurru language, Lake Eyre Basin, South Australia. Pacific Linguistics C-128. (already on file:
sources.note: In the areal-features discussion (text line ~3544): 'Pre-stopping of nasal and lateral consonants occurs after the stressed (initial) syllable in words beginning with a consonant. Pre-stopping is optional in Diyari and closely related languages, Ngamini, Yarluyandi, Yandruwantha and Yawarawarrka.' An oblique implication of initial stress for Ngamini/Yarluyandi, framed from Arabana-Wangkangurru.

sources.citation: Austin, Peter. 1991. The Karangura language. Records of the South Australian Museum 25(2), 129-137.
sources.note: Karangura (one of the three varieties under this glottocode) is known only from Wells 1894, Schoknecht and Reuther word lists; analysed by comparison with Ngamini and Diyari. No stress statement (only a remark that Wells wrote a special symbol for the low vowel 'primarily in unstressed syllables'). scanned (image PDF, tesseract 300 dpi).

sources.citation: Austin, Peter. 1988. Phonological voicing contrasts in Australian Aboriginal languages. La Trobe University Working Papers in Linguistics 1, 17-42 (author's 2020 re-typeset PDF).
sources.note: Sec. 3.5.3 Ngamini and 3.5.4 Yarluyandi describe voicing-contrast distribution and lexically diffusing trill release (from Austin's fieldnotes plus Breen's data); nothing on stress placement in Ngamini. Only for Yandruwandha does it quote Breen: voicing contrast 'only after stressed vowels (and almost always after a primary stressed vowel)', summarised as 'after the first (stressed) vowel of a word'.
